story: Jupiter's moon Ganymede shatters our expectations of planetary scale. Larger in diameter than Mercury and dwarf planet Pluto, Ganymede is the solar system's biggest moon, yet its most stunning secret remained hidden until NASA's Galileo spacecraft swept past it in 1996. Galileo detected something never before observed around a natural satellite: an internally generated magnetic field strong enough to carve out its own miniature magnetosphere embedded within Jupiter's immense radiation belts. Powered by a churning, liquid metallic core, this magnetic shield generates twin ribbons of glowing auroras encircling Ganymede's icy poles. When astronomers used the Hubble Space Telescope to watch these auroral belts rock under Jupiter's influence, their subtle motion revealed something even deeper: a subterranean saltwater ocean holding more water than all of Earth's oceans combined. Locked in a precise orbital resonance with Europa and Io, this mammoth moon behaves far more like a fully fledged planet.
angle: Ganymede is larger than Mercury and is the only moon in the solar system that generates its own magnetic field, complete with polar auroras and its own magnetosphere.
disputed: Surface proportions: Source [S1] states that bright grooved terrain covers two-thirds of the surface, whereas Source [S2] states the surface is 40% dark and 60% light grooved terrain. Scripts should state that grooved terrain covers roughly 60 to 70 percent of the surface.

First human observation: Chinese historical records report astronomer Gan De observed a companion to Jupiter in 365 BC, which may have been Ganymede, though telescopic discovery in 1610 by Galileo Galilei and Simon Marius is the standard confirmed record. Scripts should attribute the 365 BC sighting as an unverified ancient account.
